strengths: Addresses a clearly identified and well-motivated gap: no prior sample complexity results exist for constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs) under the generative model, despite this being resolved for unconstrained AMDPs and discounted CMDPs.

Provides both upper bounds (relaxed and strict feasibility) and a matching minimax lower bound for the strict feasibility setting, yielding the first near-optimal characterization of CAMDP sample complexity with respect to S, A, B, H, and the Slater constant ζ.

The algorithmic approach (reduction to a sequence of empirical discounted MDPs solved via a primal-dual/dual-descent scheme, combined with reward perturbation to handle multichain structure) is a reasonable and technically sound synthesis of techniques from Zurek & Chen (2024) and Vaswani et al. (2022).

The paper explicitly separates relaxed and strict feasibility regimes and shows a provable ζ^{-2} separation between them, which is a nice conceptual contribution mirroring but extending the discounted-case result.

Lower bound constructions are nontrivial extensions of prior hard-instance designs (from unconstrained AMDP and discounted CMDP work) to capture the interaction between diameter/transient time and the Slater margin via an amplified constraint reward; both a weakly-communicating-specific and a general-MDP lower bound are given.

Detailed, apparently careful proofs are provided in the appendix, including auxiliary lemmas for converting between average and discounted settings and controlling concentration errors, plus sample complexity bounds for estimating the auxiliary quantities B and H themselves.
weaknesses: No empirical validation whatsoever; while this is a purely theoretical paper, even simple simulations verifying the qualitative scaling with ε, ζ, B, H would strengthen confidence in the correctness/tightness of the derived rates.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the algorithm is essentially a direct combination of Zurek & Chen's (2024) discounted-reduction/perturbation technique for unconstrained AMDPs with Vaswani et al.'s (2022) dual-descent primal-dual scheme for discounted CMDPs, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

No matching lower bound is given for the relaxed feasibility setting (only strict feasibility is shown to be minimax-optimal), leaving an unresolved gap regarding whether the ζ-independent O(SA(B+H)/ε^2) relaxed bound is actually tight, or whether the omission of ζ from the upper bound conceals looseness.

The algorithm requires prior knowledge of ζ, B, and H to set numerous hyperparameters (U, ε_l, T, γ, ω, b'); although the authors note ζ can be estimated, the sample/complexity cost of jointly estimating all these quantities in a fully adaptive algorithm is not folded into a single end-to-end guarantee, limiting practical applicability.

The presentation is extremely dense with many nested constants and proof sketches deferred to a lengthy appendix; the main text would benefit from more intuition about why the reduction and error decomposition work, particularly for a broader audience less familiar with Zurek & Chen (2024) and Vaswani et al. (2022).

Limited discussion/comparison with Bai et al. (2024), the only other work on CAMDPs in the average-reward regime; the distinction between their asymptotic regret guarantees and this paper's finite-sample results could be elaborated further to better contextualize the contribution's significance.

strengths: Fills a genuine and clearly-motivated gap in the literature: while sample complexity for unconstrained average-reward MDPs (Zurek & Chen 2024) and discounted CMDPs (Vaswani et al. 2022) were previously established, no sample complexity results existed for constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs); this paper provides the first such characterization.

Provides both relaxed and strict feasibility upper bounds and matching (up to log factors) minimax lower bounds, giving a fairly complete picture of the statistical difficulty of the problem in terms of bias span H, transient time B, and Slater margin ζ.

The technical core — a 'cross-signal concentration' theorem that controls only the finite family of empirical Lagrangian oracle policies actually produced by the algorithm (via a state-action absorbing reduction plus an instance-dependent Bernstein hierarchy) — is a genuinely useful device for avoiding costly uniform concentration over the full deterministic policy class, and is nontrivial given the lack of Bellman contraction in the average-reward setting.

Two distinct, carefully constructed hard instance families (a weakly-communicating routing-tree family giving the H-scale bound and a transient six-state family giving the B-scale bound) are combined to yield a tight worst-case lower bound for the general CAMDP class; the LP-based occupancy separation arguments are explicit and appear rigorous.

The proofs are unusually detailed and self-contained, with explicit constants and step-by-step decompositions (bridge, estimation, perturbation, optimization, sensitivity terms) supporting the main theorems, which aids verifiability.

Clear positioning relative to closely related prior work (Vaswani et al. 2022, Zurek & Chen 2024, Bai et al. 2024), with an explicit account of why existing techniques do not transfer directly to the constrained average-reward setting.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no experiments or numerical illustration of the bounds/algorithm, even on toy instances; this makes it harder to assess practical relevance, tightness of constants, or algorithmic behavior in practice.

Assumption 1 (policy-wise discounted variance condition) is central to all upper bounds but is not deeply motivated or compared against alternative/weaker conditions used in the unconstrained AMDP literature; its scope of applicability and how restrictive it is in practice is not discussed.

The algorithm and analysis are a substantial but largely incremental synthesis of existing tools (Li et al. 2020 instance-dependent plug-in bounds, Vaswani et al. 2022 primal-dual/absorbing-state techniques, Zurek & Chen 2024 span/transient analysis); while the combination is nontrivial, the paper could more explicitly delineate which technical steps are genuinely new versus adapted.

No discussion of computational cost of the algorithm (grid size |Λ| = O(poly(1/ε)) or O(poly(1/(εζ))), number of discounted MDP solves T, etc.), nor any discussion of practical/implementation considerations or limitations.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, which may limit accessibility; a higher-level intuition section connecting the technical lemmas to the overall proof strategy would improve clarity for readers outside this specific subarea.

The lower bound constructions, while rigorous, rely on fairly specific/stylized instance families (three- and six-state gadgets); it is not fully discussed whether the ζ^{-2} separation between relaxed and strict feasibility is an artifact of the construction or a more fundamental phenomenon beyond this particular family.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine open problem: sample complexity of constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs) under a generative model had not been characterized before, extending both the unconstrained average-reward line (Zurek & Chen, 2024) and the discounted constrained line (Vaswani et al., 2022).

The technical machinery for cross-signal concentration (Theorem 2) that controls only the finite, data-dependent family of Lagrangian oracle policies actually produced by the algorithm—rather than requiring uniform concentration over the entire (exponentially large) deterministic policy class—is a nontrivial and reasonably novel technical device (row-decoupling via a state-action absorbing construction plus a simultaneous action-gap argument).

The paper provides matching (up to log factors) upper and lower bounds for both relaxed and strict feasibility regimes, including a careful separation showing the additional ζ^{-2} dependence is provably necessary for strict feasibility but not for relaxed feasibility.

The lower bound constructions (weakly communicating hard family with calibrated diameter/span, and a transient hard family under balanced sampling) are carefully worked out with explicit LP calculations verifying exact Slater margins and reward/constraint gaps, and the two subfamilies are combined into a general B+H worst-case bound.
The proofs are presented with a high level of rigor and detail (explicit constants, careful case analysis in the primal-dual guarantee and suboptimality decompositions), which aids verifiability.
weaknesses: The upper bounds crucially rely on Assumption 1 (a policy-wise discounted variance condition) that is imposed as a black-box structural assumption on every deterministic policy of every instance. In contrast, the unconstrained average-reward analog (Zurek & Chen, 2024) that this paper claims to extend achieves the same order of near-optimal rate unconditionally (without such a variance assumption). The paper never discusses how restrictive Assumption 1 is for general CAMDP instances, whether it can be removed, or how it compares to the unconstrained case; this weakens the claim of a fully general 'near-optimal characterization.'

There is no empirical validation whatsoever (not even a toy simulation) to sanity-check the algorithm, the tightness of constants, or whether Assumption 1 is easy or hard to satisfy in practice. For a paper proposing a concrete algorithm (not purely an information-theoretic existence result), this is a notable gap.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, with very little intuition given for why the cross-signal concentration argument works, why the specific perturbation/rounding/grid constructions (ω, Λ, rounding map) are necessary, or what practical insight the reader should take away; this hurts accessibility and makes it hard to assess robustness of the argument outside of trusting the line-by-line algebra.

The lower bound theorems are stated only up to universal (unspecified) constants c0, c1, c2, c3, and the regime of validity (small ε, small ζ, large D) is fairly restrictive; there is no discussion of the gap region (e.g., moderate ζ or ε) where the bounds may not apply, nor any discussion of how loose the log factors might be in practice.

The algorithm's computational complexity (solving T = O(ε^{-4}) or O((ε²ζ⁴)^{-1}) sequential discounted LPs/planning problems) is not discussed at all; the contribution is purely about sample complexity, but computational tractability is a natural concern for a 'model-based primal-dual algorithm' and is left completely unaddressed.

The scope of the contribution is narrow and highly specialized (a specific corner of constrained average-reward RL theory), and the significance/impact for the broader community is not strongly argued beyond stating that this is 'the first' such characterization; there is limited discussion of implications for algorithm design, follow-up open problems, or practical relevance beyond the introduction's brief motivating examples.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously open problem: sample complexity of constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs) under a generative model, extending both discounted-CMDP results (Vaswani et al. 2022) and unconstrained-AMDP results (Zurek & Chen 2024) to a harder joint setting.

Provides matching (up to log factors) upper and lower bounds for both relaxed feasibility (O(SA(B+H)/eps^2)) and strict feasibility (O(SA(B+H)/(eps^2 zeta^2))), giving a near-minimax-optimal characterization and a clean, provable separation between the two feasibility regimes.

Introduces a nontrivial technical device -- the 'cross-signal concentration' theorem that controls only the finite family of empirical Lagrangian oracle policies actually produced by the algorithm (via row decoupling / state-action absorbing construction and a Bernstein hierarchy), avoiding a costly uniform bound over the entire deterministic policy class.

Careful minimax lower bound construction combining two complementary hard families (a weakly-communicating routing-tree family for the H-scale bound and a six-state transient family for the B-scale bound under balanced sampling), which is a nice technical contribution in its own right.

The paper is thorough and internally consistent: detailed appendices with full proofs, explicit constants, and calibration of diameter/transient-time/bias-span parameters for the hard instances, lending credibility to the claimed rates.
weaknesses: Purely theoretical contribution with no empirical validation or even illustrative numerical simulation of the algorithm/rates, making it hard to assess practical relevance or tightness of constants/log factors.

Assumption 1 (policy-wise discounted variance condition) is central to all upper bounds but is somewhat opaque; the paper offers no discussion of which MDP classes satisfy it, how restrictive it is relative to standard weakly-communicating/multichain conditions, or examples where it fails.

The algorithm assumes structural quantities H, B, and the Slater margin ζ (or a valid lower bound) are supplied in advance; there is no discussion of how these would be estimated or of the added complexity/adaptivity this would require in practice.

The general lower bound matching the strict-feasibility upper bound requires restricting to 'balanced' generative-model algorithms; the paper does not fully address whether unbalanced/fully adaptive strategies could beat this rate, leaving a gap between the adaptive weakly-communicating result and the fully general combined bound.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy in the main text, with most proofs and even some key definitions relegated to a very long appendix; more intuition/discussion in the main body (e.g., why the ζ^{-2} dependence is unavoidable, or a sketch of why cross-signal concentration suffices) would improve accessibility.

Discussion of related work such as Bai et al. (2024), which also studies CAMDPs, is brief; a more detailed technical comparison (e.g., why their techniques cannot yield finite-sample generative-model rates) would strengthen the positioning claim of being 'first'.

The construction restricts optimizers to support size at most two and external mixtures with a specific structure; while likely standard, the justification is terse and could benefit from more explicit discussion in the main paper.
